title: Quick Guide to Mince Lemongrass with Herb Shears for Thai Soups
meta_description: Learn how to mince lemongrass with herb scissors for authentic Thai soups. This quick guide covers technique, tips, and why Herb Scissors are a game‑changer.
html:
When you need to mince lemongrass with herb scissors for a Thai soup, the right tool can shave minutes off prep and keep the flavor bright. Lemongrass is tough to bite‑size chop with a knife, but a set of five‑blade herb shears tackles it in one snip, delivering fine, uniform pieces that release their citrusy aroma instantly.

Why Traditional Knife Work Falls Short

Even the sharpest chef’s knife struggles with the fibrous stalk of lemongrass. You often end up with uneven chunks, and the extra force can bruise the delicate inner cores, dulling the fresh zing you want in a broth. Herb scissors solve these problems by:

  • Providing multiple blades that cut simultaneously, reducing crushing.
  • Creating consistent, bite‑size pieces that distribute flavor evenly.
  • Requiring less hand pressure, which preserves the bright aroma.

Because the blades are spaced just right, the stalk is minced without the need to peel or trim extensively—perfect for quick weeknight cooking.

Getting Started: Preparing Lemongrass for the Shears

Before you reach for your herb scissors, a few simple steps ensure a clean mince:

  1. Trim the outer layers. Peel away the dry, papery skin until you expose the pale, tender inner stalk.
  2. Snap off the root end. The bottom is woody and won't cut well; discard it.
  3. Cut to length. For most Thai soups, a 4‑inch piece is ideal. Slice the stalk into 1‑inch sections—these become the pieces you’ll feed into the scissors.

Once the stalk is trimmed, you can feed each segment straight into the Herb Scissors. No need to chop further; the five blades will do the work.

How to Mince Lemongrass with Herb Scissors

Using herb scissors is intuitive. Hold the stalk firmly in one hand and close the blades with the other. The five‑blade configuration slices the lemongrass into tiny ribbons with each squeeze. Here’s the step‑by‑step:

  • Place the trimmed lemongrass segment between the blades, aligning it with the cutting edge.
  • Close the scissors completely; the blades will intersect the stalk, creating a fine mince.
  • Open the scissors and shake the minced pieces into a bowl or directly into your soup pot.

For larger batches, repeat the motion without resetting the stalk—just slide it forward a little each time. The result is a uniform, aromatic mince that melts into the broth.

Cleaning and Maintaining Your Herb Scissors

After a session of mincing lemongrass, the blades can retain bits of fibrous material. The built‑in cleaning comb on the Herb Scissors makes maintenance a breeze. Simply run the comb along the blades to dislodge any residue, then rinse under warm water. Dry the scissors thoroughly to prevent rust, and store them in a dry drawer or hanging rack.

Because the scissor design is stainless steel, it resists corrosion, but regular cleaning keeps the cutting edge sharp and ready for the next herb—whether it’s cilantro, chives, or basil.

Integrating Minced Lemongrass into Thai Soups

Now that you’ve mastered the technique, here’s how to use that minced lemongrass for maximum flavor:

  • Tom Yum. Add the mince during the simmering stage, letting it steep for 3‑5 minutes before serving.
  • Tom Kha Gai. Stir the minced stalk into the coconut broth right after the galangal and kaffir lime leaves, then let it infuse.
  • Spicy Lemongrass Soup. Combine the mince with chicken or pork stock, chilies, and fish sauce for a quick, aromatic bowl.

Because the pieces are so fine, they won’t interrupt the smooth texture of the soup, yet they will deliver that signature citrus punch that defines Thai cuisine.

Tips for Consistent Results

Even with the best tool, a few habits improve the outcome:

  • Use fresh lemongrass. Older stalks become woody and harder to cut.
  • Don’t overload the scissors. One or two segments at a time keep the blades from jamming.
  • Maintain blade sharpness. If the scissors start to feel “sticky,” a quick honing with a fine sharpening stone restores their edge.

Following these simple practices ensures that each batch of mince lemongrass with herb scissors is as bright and fragrant as the first.

FAQ

Can I use herb scissors on other tough herbs?

Yes. The five‑blade design works well on cilantro, chives, basil, and even mint. The same technique—trim, slice, and snip—applies across most leafy herbs.

Do the scissors cut through the hard root end of lemongrass?

The root end is too dense for the blades. Trim it off before using the scissors; the remaining stalk will mince smoothly.

Is the cleaning comb enough to keep the blades hygienic?

The comb removes most debris, but a quick rinse and a wipe with a damp cloth after each use ensures the blades stay clean and rust‑free.
